title: Kulintang (gong-chime row)
summary: The kulintang is a row of eight small bossed gongs laid on a frame, lowest on the player's left, struck with two wooden beaters. One player leads the melody on the row while large hanging gongs, a single-headed drum and a small timekeeping gong hold the cycle underneath.
howToPlay: Eight gongs lie in a row, numbered from the low gong on the left to the high gong on the right; three more pieces stand for the large gong, the drum and the small timekeeping gong.
Notes travel around the ring. Strike each piece as its mark reaches the line, on the beat or on the half beat.
Three patterns are offered, from slow and steady to quick and showy; each runs twice.
rules: Eight gongs are tuned to a five-note scale with unequal steps, so the row climbs a little more than an octave and a half.
The large gong marks the start of each cycle; the drum and the small gong fill the beats in between.
A stroke on the beat scores in full, a near stroke scores less, and an extra stroke costs a little.
Each pattern repeats twice; the round ends when the last stroke is judged.
heritageNote: The kulintang is best known among the Maguindanao and Maranao peoples of Mindanao in the southern Philippines, and similar gong rows are played by neighbouring communities in Sulu, Sabah, Brunei and further east. It is played at weddings, festivals and welcomes, in slower old styles and quicker, freely varied newer ones.
